Architecture overview and decisions\n\n```\nprofile.Driver == \"cockroach\"\n        │\n        ├── store/db/db.go factory ──► postgres.NewCockroachDB(profile)   (new, same package as NewDB)\n        │                                   │\n        │                                   ├── shared DSN builder (postgres.go) — COCKROACH_DSN, simple_protocol\n        │                                   ├── shared pool settings (postgres.go) — 10/5/5m/1m + 60s ping\n        │                                   └── shared SQL implementation files (23 files, unchanged)\n        │\n        ├── store/migrator.go ──► migration/cockroach/{0.19…0.35,LATEST.sql}  (mirrors postgres dirs)\n        │         └── Cockroach branch: no Begin(); inject SET serial_normalization; whole-file Exec\n        │\n        └── runtime retries ──► crdb.ExecuteTx wrapper around 8 BeginTx sites (cockroach-only)\n```\n\n- REPOSITORY FACT: driver factory switch at `store/db/db.go` (`case \"sqlite\"`, `case \"mysql\"`, `case \"postgres\"`, default error); a `case \"cockroach\"` is added.\n- REPOSITORY FACT: `NewDB` at `store/db/postgres/postgres.go:22`; appends `default_query_exec_mode=simple_protocol` (line 33); `MaxOpenConns(10)` (line 42), `MaxIdleConns(5)`, `ConnMaxLifetime(5m)`, `ConnMaxIdleTime(1m)`, 60s ping.\n\n### 5.1 D1 — Whole-file migration execution, no explicit transaction (Q1)\nREPOSITORY FACT: `store/migrator.go:321-335` — `execute()` runs the entire file via one `tx.ExecContext(ctx, stmt)`; no splitter exists. DOCUMENTATION FACT: simple-protocol multi-statement strings support automatic retries; most DDL cannot run in explicit transactions and `autocommit_before_ddl` commits before DDL regardless. INFERENCE: `Begin()` adds no atomicity on Cockroach and misleads readers; the Cockroach branch drops it.\n\n### 5.2 D2 — `SET serial_normalization = 'sql_sequence'` injected by the migrator (Q2)\nDOCUMENTATION FACT: session variable controlling SERIAL handling in table definitions. REPOSITORY FACT: all IDs are `int32`; default `rowid` mode yields 64-bit `unique_rowid()` values (DOCUMENTATION FACT). INFERENCE: `sql_sequence` is required to keep IDs in int32 range (sequences start at 1); a hard compatibility requirement.\n\n### 5.3 D3 — Mirror versioned migration directories (Q3)\nREPOSITORY FACT: base path `migration/{driver}/` (`migrator.go:210`); `GetCurrentSchemaVersion` scans `*/*.sql` (line 257); version parse (line 300); history upsert only after success (lines 142-149, 192-199). INFERENCE: mirrored `store/migration/cockroach/` works with zero migrator-structure changes beyond the Cockroach branch.\n\n### 5.4 D4 — simple_protocol everywhere (Q4)\nREPOSITORY FACT: `postgres.go:33` forces simple protocol today. INFERENCE: identical runtime behavior, zero protocol coupling, smallest test surface. The review's split-protocol idea is deferred with a benchmark gate (§16).\n\n### 5.5 D5 — `crdb.ExecuteTx` retry wrapper on 8 tx sites (Q5)\nREPOSITORY FACT: `cockroach-go/v2 v2.4.3` in `go.mod`; `ExecuteTx(ctx, *sql.DB, opts, fn)` exists in v2.4.3 (module cache `crdb/tx.go:299`); precedent at `vectordb_cockroach.go:191`; `isPostgresRetryable` string-matching at `bridge.go:320` does not match CRDB 40001 messages. INFERENCE: SQLSTATE-based retry supersedes the string hack on the Cockroach path.\n\n### 5.6 D6 — `postgres.NewCockroachDB()` (Q6)\nSame package, shared internals (per §4). No `store/db/cockroach/` directory is created (REPOSITORY FACT: none exists today).\n\n### 5.7 D7 — `COCKROACH_DSN`, no fallback (Q7)\nREPOSITORY FACT: `internal/profile/profile.go` carries `Driver`/`DSN`; `bin/memos/main.go` binds them via viper. INFERENCE: explicit DSN prevents cross-wiring; fail-fast at startup. REPOSITORY FACT: existing Cockroach tooling is reused — `scripts/docker-compose.cockroach.yml` (`bchat_user`/`bchat_pass`@`localhost:26257/bchat?sslmode=disable`, console :8080), Taskfile `build:cockroach`/`run:cockroach`/`crdb:check`/`crdb:db-check`/`crdb:test`/`crdb:docker:build`/`crdb:docker:run` (build tag `cockroach`).\n\n---\n\n## 6. SQL portability audit (construct → usage → support → action)\n\n| Construct | Usage in bchat | Cockroach support | Action |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| `SERIAL PRIMARY KEY` | every table, `LATEST.sql` | supported; mode = session var | inject SET (D2); prove via P1 |\n| `EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM NOW())` BIGINT defaults | 19× in `LATEST.sql`; runtime relies on default (`migration_history.go:39-45`) | `extract → float`; no implicit float→int8 assignment | `::BIGINT` in Cockroach DDL; prove via P3 |\n| `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` | `agent.go:2773-2781` (single statement, no tx) | supported (v23.2+) | none (note #167582) |\n| `FOR UPDATE` | `bridge.go:356,500` (in tx) | supported | none (retry wrapper handles 40001) |\n| `RETURNING` | ~20+ sites | supported | none |\n| `ON CONFLICT` | `LATEST.sql:208`; `migration_history.go:39` | supported | none |\n| `ILIKE` | `memo_filter.go:143,172,209,224` | supported | none |\n| `jsonb` + `@>` | `memo_filter.go` | supported | none |\n| `::BOOLEAN` / `::BIGINT` casts | `memo.go:106-115`; `agent.go:2605,2693,2718,2776,2780` | supported (explicit casts) | none |\n| `UPDATE … FROM` | legacy `0.24/01__memo_pinned.sql` (never runs on Cockroach — §7.4) | supported (v23.1+) | allowed; review-required in drift check |\n| `CREATE VECTOR INDEX` | `vectordb_cockroach.go:109` (runtime) | supported; **no `IF NOT EXISTS`** | runtime-only; already handled |\n| `INSERT … $6::VECTOR` / `<=>` | `vectordb_cockroach.go:194,323-327` | supported | none |\n| DDL in explicit tx | `migrator.go:91,178` | not supported (mostly) | no `Begin()` for Cockroach |\n| Forbidden constructs (drift check) | none found in repo (verified) | see §10 | CI gate |\n\n**Implementation step 6.1 (audit gate):** a full statement-by-statement `diff` between every `store/migration/postgres/**/*.sql` file and its Cockroach mirror must be performed in Phase 2. The only anticipated textual differences: `::BIGINT` on the 19 EXTRACT defaults.\n\n---\n\n## 7. Migration execution design\n\n### 7.1 Current behavior (Postgres, unchanged)\nREPOSITORY FACT (`store/migrator.go`): `preMigrate` applies `LATEST.sql` inside `Begin()` when no history exists (lines 160-207); `Migrate` applies versioned files `> latestMigrationHistoryVersion` inside `Begin()` (lines 62-150); `execute()` tolerates \"duplicate column\"/\"already exists\"/\"column already exists\" errors (lines 321-335); history upsert only after batch success (lines 142-149).\n\n### 7.2 New behavior (Cockroach)\n1. Read files from `migration/cockroach/` (D3).\n2. No `Begin()`/`Commit()`.\n3. Prepend `SET serial_normalization = 'sql_sequence';` (D2) to the file content, then `db.ExecContext` the batch on one connection.\n4. All version logic, skip logic, history upsert, and idempotent tolerance unchanged.\n\nDOCUMENTATION FACT: sending the batch as one unit over the simple protocol allows statement-level automatic retries; DDL executes as individual online schema changes with `autocommit_before_ddl` committing prior statements first.\n\n### 7.3 Atomicity — explicit discussion (review Issue 3, retained)\n- **Changed vs Postgres:** failed statement N no longer rolls back statements 1..N-1.\n- **Required by Cockroach:** online schema changes do not support all-or-nothing multi-statement DDL; keeping `Begin()` would be cosmetic.\n- **Safe for bchat because:**\n  1. `migration_history` is written only after full success (`migrator.go:142-149`) → failed boot re-runs the migration.\n  2. All DDL is `IF NOT EXISTS` (REPOSITORY FACT: `LATEST.sql`); the only data statement is `ON CONFLICT (tenant_id, code) DO NOTHING` (`LATEST.sql:201-208`). **The LATEST.sql file is fully idempotent** — verified statement-by-statement (REPOSITORY FACT, new in v4).\n  3. `execute()` swallows \"already exists\" class errors (`migrator.go:326-330`).\n  4. Fresh Cockroach deployments run `LATEST.sql` only (§7.4), so no partial-history recovery exists in the field at first deploy.\n\n### 7.4 Which files actually execute on Cockroach (new in v4 — repository-derived)\nREPOSITORY FACT (`migrator.go`): on a fresh database, `preMigrate` applies `LATEST.sql`, then upserts history = `schemaVersion` (0.35). `Migrate` then applies only versioned files **greater than** the latest history version. Therefore:\n- **On a fresh Cockroach deployment: only `LATEST.sql` executes.** The versioned dirs `0.19/`…`0.35/` never execute; they exist solely to satisfy the version machinery (`GetCurrentSchemaVersion` scans `*/*.sql`, `migrator.go:257`) and parity validation.\n- **On future upgrades (0.36+): only the new files execute.**\n- Consequences (INFERENCE):\n  1. The legacy data-backfill statements in 0.19–0.24 (e.g., the random-UUID `UPDATE memo SET resource_name = uuid_in(md5(random()::text || random()::text)::cstring)` at `0.19/00__add_resource_name.sql:3` — **non-idempotent**, would rewrite values on re-run) are **inert on Cockroach**. They are mirrored file-for-file for parity but never run.\n  2. The idempotency rule (§7.5) governs only **future** Cockroach migrations (0.36+), where the recovery scenario actually applies.\n\n### 7.5 Recovery after partially applied migration (plan3_review #2)\n\nScenario: future incremental migration `0.36/00__x.sql` fails at statement 4; statements 1–3 applied; history row NOT written; developer edits the file; redeploy.\n\n**Recovery procedure (ordered):**\n1. **Detect:** boot fails with the migration error; `migration_history` has no 0.36 row (REPOSITORY FACT: upsert happens only after success). Logs identify the failing statement.\n2. **Assess:** determine which statements applied via `SELECT * FROM migration_history;` plus `SHOW TABLES` / `information_schema` inspection (the `crdb:sql:shell` target).\n3. **Two allowed paths:**\n   - **Path A — idempotent file (default):** fix the failing statement in the unreleased file, redeploy. All applied statements re-execute safely because the file is idempotent (§7.3 items 2-3). This is the required norm for all Cockroach migrations.\n   - **Path B — non-idempotent data transform:** if a transform is not idempotent (e.g., random-value UPDATE), the file **must not be edited in place** after any statement applied. Instead: (a) leave the file as-is, (b) add a NEW file `0.36/01__fix.sql` that compensates or completes the transform, (c) redeploy. Editing applied files is prohibited (see below).\n4. **Escalation — fresh deployment only:** because Cockroach has no production data at first deploy (INFERENCE: first deployment is the initial Fly.io rollout), a stuck migration can also be resolved by dropping and re-creating the database, then redeploying. This option is *not* available once production data exists.\n\n**Migration file lifecycle rule (new, enforced by §10 drift policy and code review):**\n- Files that have never succeeded (no history row) may be edited freely within the same development cycle.\n- Once a file has a history row, **never edit it** — all fixes ship as new files (Path B). This protects both Postgres (whose atomic migrations make editing retroactive and untested) and Cockroach (whose partial application makes editing dangerous).\n- Every Cockroach migration must be idempotent: DDL with `IF NOT EXISTS`, inserts with `ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING`, transforms with deterministic, WHERE-guarded values. The 0.19 random-UUID pattern is the canonical counter-example and is banned going forward.\n\n---\n\n## 8. Runtime driver design\n\n### 8.1 Constructor and factory\nNew: `postgres.NewCockroachDB(profile *profile.Profile) (store.Driver, error)`; new factory case in `store/db/db.go`. REPOSITORY FACT: `store/driver.go` interface needs no changes — the same 23 implementation files already satisfy it.\n\n### 8.2 DSN\n`COCKROACH_DSN` env var (D7), no fallback. Reuse the DSN builder (`postgres.go:33` appends `simple_protocol`). Local: `scripts/docker-compose.cockroach.yml` credentials, `sslmode=disable`. Production (Fly.io + CockroachDB Cloud): `postgresql://user:pass@host:26257/bchat?sslmode=verify-full` per `bugs/057/prod_checklist.md`. Fail-fast when `--driver=cockroach` and DSN empty.\n\n### 8.3 Pool settings (plan3_review #9)\n- **Decision:** preserve the existing defaults initially — `MaxOpenConns(10)`, `MaxIdleConns(5)`, `ConnMaxLifetime(5m)`, `ConnMaxIdleTime(1m)`, 60s ping (REPOSITORY FACT: `postgres.go:42-48`).\n- **Rationale reframed (per review):** these are **operational tuning parameters, not architecture**. DOCUMENTATION FACT: active connections across all pools should not greatly exceed ~4× cluster vCPUs. The correct validation point is the production cluster sizing exercise at deploy time (Phase 7), where `MaxOpenConns` is adjusted via configuration if the Cloud cluster is small. No code-level sizing logic (e.g., `runtime.NumCPU()`) is introduced.\n\n### 8.4 Vector database\nREPOSITORY FACT: `vectordb_cockroach.go` already implements the native `VECTOR(1536)` provider (constructor line 27; runtime `CREATE TABLE` + `CREATE VECTOR INDEX` lines 82-113; `crdb.ExecuteTx` upserts lines 191-218; `<=>` search lines 323-327). No changes. Review Issue 5 justification (retained): the schema exists only when the vector capability is compiled in (build tag `cockroach`; env gate `VECTOR_DB_PROVIDER=cockroach` per Taskfile `crdb:check`), so runtime creation is the correct boundary.\n\n---\n\n## 9. Transaction retry design (review Issue 6, extended per plan3_review #3)\n\n### 9.1 Inventory of explicit transactions\n\n| # | Site | Function | Transaction body |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| 1 | `bridge.go:112` | `createBridgeHandoffAttempt` | UPDATE lock, COUNT, MAX+1, INSERT; post-commit read |\n| 2 | `bridge.go:356` | `CreateBridgeHandoffReplyIfActive` | `SELECT … FOR UPDATE`, INSERT, idempotent constraint branch |\n| 3 | `bridge.go:500` | `CreateBridgeHandoffReplyAndOutboxIfActive` | `FOR UPDATE`, INSERT reply, INSERT outbox |\n| 4 | `bridge.go:726` | `ClaimPendingBridgeReplyOutbox` | batch claim UPDATEs on status/expiry conditions |\n| 5 | `bridge.go:818` | `CompleteClaimedBridgeReplyOutbox` | SELECT, UPDATE, idempotent branch |\n| 6 | `bridge.go:912` | `FailClaimedBridgeReplyOutbox` | SELECT, UPDATE, idempotent branch |\n| 7 | `bridge.go:1003` | `ClaimBridgeReplyOutboxByOutboxID` | SELECT, claim UPDATE |\n| 8 | `agent.go:772` | `CreateAgentMessages` | batch INSERT loop |\n\nPlus non-transactional: `agent.go:2773-2781` `ClaimPendingEvents` — single `UPDATE … FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED … RETURNING` (server-retried implicit transaction; no wrapper needed).\n\n### 9.2 Side-effect audit (review Issue 6) — retained from v3\nAll 8 transaction bodies are pure DB operations; external effects (websocket delivery, outbox processing, HTTP responses) occur after `Commit()` in callers. `uuid.NewString()` regenerates harmlessly on retry. A code-review checklist item enforces \"no I/O inside tx closures\" (§18).\n\n### 9.3 Determinism classification under retry (plan3_review #3, new)\n\nMechanical fact: a 40001 aborts and rolls back the failed attempt's writes, so **a retried closure never double-writes**. The only variability across attempts is that *reads may observe newer committed state*. Classification per site:\n\n| Site | Classification | Why it is safe |\n|---|---|---|\n| 1 `createBridgeHandoffAttempt` (112) | **optimistic by design** | `MAX(generation)+1` recomputed on retry; monotonic guard; conflict errors preserved. Generation is only meaningful within the tx |\n| 2 `CreateBridgeHandoffReplyIfActive` (356) | **may observe newer state; guard-safe** | re-reads `FOR UPDATE` row; if handoff deactivated meanwhile, returns `ErrBridgeHandoffConflict` — correct outcome |\n| 3 `CreateBridgeHandoffReplyAndOutboxIfActive` (500) | **may observe newer state; guard-safe** | same pattern + outbox insert is append-only |\n| 4 `ClaimPendingBridgeReplyOutbox` (726) | **may observe newer state; guard-safe** | claim UPDATEs guarded by `status`/`expiry` conditions; rows claimed by others are excluded on re-read |\n| 5 `CompleteClaimedBridgeReplyOutbox` (818) | **deterministic under retry** | UPDATE guarded by `claim_token`; idempotent completion branch handles the already-completed case |\n| 6 `FailClaimedBridgeReplyOutbox` (912) | **deterministic under retry** | same token-guarded pattern with idempotent fail branch |\n| 7 `ClaimBridgeReplyOutboxByOutboxID` (1003) | **may observe newer state; guard-safe** | claim UPDATE guarded by status conditions |\n| 8 `CreateAgentMessages` (772) | **deterministic under retry** | append-only INSERTs; failed attempt's inserts were rolled back |\n\nConclusion: no site produces different *results* across retries in a way that changes observable behavior beyond the intended \"claim once\" semantics; sites 1–4 may legitimately observe newer state, which is by design. This classification is recorded in a table comment at each wrapper site during implementation.\n\n### 9.4 Wrapper mechanics (cockroach-only)\n- Convert the 8 sites to `func(tx *sql.Tx) error` closures run via `crdb.ExecuteTx(ctx, d.db, nil, fn)` (API: module cache `crdb/tx.go:299`, v2.4.3; precedent `vectordb_cockroach.go:191`).\n- `crdb.ExecuteTx` detects SQLSTATE 40001/40003/08xxx and re-runs with backoff (DOCUMENTATION FACT: client retry handling; MCP §2.2 row 6).\n- Non-retryable errors propagate; `store.ErrBridge*` sentinels untouched.\n- `isPostgresRetryable` loop at `bridge.go:95-104` stays for Postgres; the Cockroach path does not reach it.\n- `RunResiliently` (`resilience.go`, zero callers — REPOSITORY FACT) stays unused; deferred (§16).\n\n---\n\n## 10. Capability drift policy (plan3_review #4 and #5)\n\nGoal: keep Postgres ↔ Cockroach divergence continuous and documented, not a one-time audit.\n\n### 10.1 Rules\n1. **Every new SQL feature** (in migrations or runtime queries) must update the capability matrix (§3) in the same change.\n2. **Every new migration file** must pass the portability audit (§6) and the drift check below before merge.\n3. **CI rejects undocumented divergence**: a file cannot add a construct from the FORBIDDEN list at all; from the REVIEW-REQUIRED list without an explicit `--verified` annotation in the capability matrix.\n4. **Never edit an applied migration file** (§7.5 lifecycle rule).\n\n### 10.2 Drift-check construct list (MCP-verified, §2.2)\n\n**FORBIDDEN in Cockroach migration files (CI fails):**\n- `CREATE EXTENSION` (not fully supported)\n- `LISTEN` / `NOTIFY` / `UNLISTEN` (not implemented)\n- advisory lock functions (`pg_advisory_lock*`) (unsupported; no-op stubs)\n- `CREATE DOMAIN` (unsupported)\n- range types, `MACADDR`, `MONEY` (unsupported)\n- triggers (`CREATE TRIGGER`) (unsupported)\n- `DEFERRABLE` / `INITIALLY DEFERRED` constraints (unsupported)\n- `DROP PRIMARY KEY` / dropping the primary key constraint (unsupported; use drop+add in one transaction)\n- PL/pgSQL blocks (`DO $$`, functions with body syntax) (partial/unimplemented)\n- Procedural blocks of any kind — migrations must be plain SQL\n\n**REVIEW-REQUIRED (CI flags for human sign-off, then annotate the matrix):**\n- `ALTER TYPE` (supported v23.1+; `DROP VALUE` spawns non-cancellable jobs)\n- `UPDATE … FROM` (supported; join-output ambiguity)\n- `COPY` (supported generally, but `IMPORT INTO` excluded on vector-indexed tables)\n- `SELECT *` in any statement that could become a prepared statement (0A000 risk)\n- Non-idempotent data transforms (random values, unguarded UPDATE)\n\n### 10.3 CI implementation (Phase 6)\nNew `scripts/validate-cockroach-compat.sh`: grep-based scanner over `store/migration/cockroach/**/*.sql` matching the lists above; exit 1 on FORBIDDEN, exit 2 on unannotated REVIEW-REQUIRED. Wired into `Taskfile.yml` (`crdb:check` extension) and the validate-parity flow. Shell-level parsing is explicitly best-effort (mirroring the existing `validate-parity.sh` limitation, line 235); regexes are documented in the script.\n\n---\n\n## 11. Rollback strategy (plan3_review #6, new)\n\n**Property: Bug 057 is additive-only.** No behavior change to the Postgres or SQLite drivers; no postgres migration file changes; `postgres.go` DSN/pool behavior unchanged (REPOSITORY FACT: v3/v4 changes touch only new files plus the cockroach branches in `db.go`, `migrator.go`, and the two tx-site files).\n\n**Rollback scenarios:**\n1. **Pre-deploy (build time):** reverting the change = reverting the commit. Nothing else required — the feature is compiled in via the `cockroach` build tag and driver flag; other builds are unaffected.\n2. **Post-deploy, runtime bug in Cockroach path:** switch `--driver` back to `postgres` (or `sqlite`) on the same binary and restart. No migration changes are needed because Postgres migrations were never touched. Cockroach data is simply unused.\n3. **Cockroach data disposal:** at first deployment there is no production data (INFERENCE: initial rollout is greenfield on CockroachDB Cloud). If the Cockroach rollout is abandoned, the cluster/database is dropped; no export or backfill obligations exist.\n4. **Future incremental migrations:** because applied files are never edited (§7.5), rollback of a released schema version means deploying the previous code version; the database stays at its last successful history version (REPOSITORY FACT: history upsert is the commit marker). No downgrade migrations are written — bchat does not ship downgrades today, and Cockroach's online schema changes make `ALTER … DROP` rollbacks a per-incident decision, not an automated path (INFERENCE; noted in §15).\n\n---\n\n## 12. Experiments — VERIFY-FIRST gates with exit criteria (plan3_review #7)\n\nAll run on single-node Docker (`scripts/docker-compose.cockroach.yml`) before implementation. Pass criteria are measurable.\n\n| ID | Question | Method | Pass criteria (all must hold) |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| P1 | Does injected `SET serial_normalization='sql_sequence'` produce `nextval(...)` defaults through the whole-file path? | Run Cockroach `LATEST.sql` (SET-prefixed) via the migrator; `SHOW CREATE TABLE` on ≥3 tables incl. `agent_tenants` and `migration_history` | 100% of SERIAL columns show `nextval('…_seq')` defaults; **0** `unique_rowid()` occurrences; migration_history row written |\n| P2 | Does whole-file exec migrate cleanly, and is failure+re-run idempotent? | Full `LATEST.sql` run; delete history row; re-run; then inject a failing statement mid-file and re-run | Re-run after history deletion is a no-op (no errors, no dupes — esp. `tenant_role_templates` stays at 5 rows); failed run writes no history row; corrected re-run completes |\n| P3 | Is `EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM NOW())::BIGINT` valid and correct as a default? | `CREATE TABLE t (c BIGINT NOT NULL DEFAULT EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM NOW())::BIGINT); INSERT INTO t DEFAULT VALUES; SELECT c;` | Insert succeeds; `c` = unix epoch seconds ±1; uncast variant fails with a type error (documents why the cast is needed) |\n| P4 | Does `crdb.ExecuteTx` retry correctly under contention? | 2–4 concurrent claimers over 1000 outbox rows (reuse claim/complete shapes of §9.1 sites 4–7); force conflicts | **1000 claims, 0 duplicated rows, 0 lost rows**; ≥1 SQLSTATE 40001 observed in logs; every retry eventually succeeds; completion count = 1000 |\n| P5 | SKIP LOCKED claim correctness under concurrency | Multiple workers on `ClaimPendingEvents` query (`agent.go:2781`) over 1000 events | Each event claimed exactly once (0 double-claims, 0 lost); workers observe different batches |\n| P6 | Vector path regression | Existing `crdb:test` suite (Taskfile `crdb:test`, `-tags cockroach`) with `VECTOR_DB_PROVIDER=cockroach` | All tests green; vector insert/search round-trip latency within 2× of pre-change baseline (informational, not a gate) |\n\n---\n\n## 13. Benchmarks — regression detection only (plan3_review #8, new)\n\nNot optimization; the goal is a documented baseline so future changes can detect regressions. A `crdb:bench` Taskfile target runs the suite on the local Docker cluster and records results in `build/bench/`:\n\n| Benchmark | Metric | Method | Baseline note |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| Migration runtime | wall time for fresh `LATEST.sql` | `time ./build/memos --driver=cockroach --mode dev` on empty DB | compare vs Postgres on the same host (informational; different engines) |\n| CreateAgentMessages TPS | inserts/sec, p99 latency | Go benchmark wrapping `CreateAgentMessages` (site 8) with N=1000 | Postgres vs Cockroach on same host |\n| Bridge outbox throughput | claim→complete cycles/sec | benchmark wrapping §9.1 sites 4–7 flow | Postgres vs Cockroach |\n| Vector search latency | p99 of `<=>` top-K query | reuse existing vector tests with 1k vectors | Cockroach-only |\n\nBenchmarks are advisory: no perf gate in CI, and no changes to the `simple_protocol` decision result from them without a follow-up decision (deferred per §16).\n\n---\n\n## 14. Adversarial pass — every behavioral change defended (retained from v3, updated)\n\n### 14.1 Migrations: explicit-transaction → autocommit whole-file\n1. **Changed:** a migration file is no longer atomic.\n2. **Required:** online schema changes do not support multi-statement DDL transactions (MCP row 4).\n3. **New failure modes:** partial application on failure → mitigated by idempotent `LATEST.sql` (verified), `execute()` tolerance, history-after-success, and §7.5 recovery procedure.\n\n### 14.2 Migrations: injected `SET serial_normalization`\n1. **Changed:** none on Postgres (cockroach-only branch).\n2. **Required:** int32 overflow with `unique_rowid()` (D2 evidence chain).\n3. **New failure modes:** SET silently not applying → gated by P1; performance: one `nextval` round-trip per insert (negligible at bchat volumes — INFERENCE); `sql_sequence_cached` is the documented alternative if ever needed.\n\n### 14.3 DDL: explicit `::BIGINT` casts\n1. **Changed:** Cockroach files differ textually (19 defaults); Postgres uses numeric→bigint assignment cast (rounds), Cockroach uses explicit float→int8 cast (truncates). ≤1s deviation possible at .5s fractional boundaries.\n2. **Required:** `extract → float` with no implicit int assignment (MCP row 3); uncast DDL fails at CREATE TABLE.\n3. **New failure modes:** none beyond DDL validation, gated by P3; runtime `migration_history.go:39` needs no change (uses the default).\n\n### 14.4 Runtime: retry closures on 8 tx sites\n1. **Changed:** 40001 re-executes the closure instead of propagating.\n2. **Required:** client-side retry handling is documented as required for 40001 (MCP row 6).\n3. **New failure modes:** duplicate side effects → none found (§9.2); Design CockroachDB deployment so that a developer already deploying to Fly.io with Neon experiences the same operational workflow. Every manual deployment step should either become a Taskfile target or be explicitly justified. Include local development, production deployment, verification, smoke testing, rollback, and environment management. The goal is that switching from Neon to CockroachDB changes infrastructure, not developer ergonomics.**

9: ## Overview

11: This guide covers deploying bchat to Fly.io using Neon serverless Postgres as the database backend. The Postgres driver is fully implemented, the Dockerfile exists, and the Taskfile is ready.

23: ## Prerequisites
24: 
25: | Requirement | Check command |
26: |-------------|--------------|
27: | `fly` CLI installed | `fly --version` |
28: | Logged into Fly.io | `fly auth whoami` |
29: | Fly app created | `fly status --app bchat-pg` |
30: | Neon account | https://console.neon.tech |

35: ## Default Credentials (Local Postgres)

37: Used for migration validation only, not for production.

39: | Field | Value |

41: | Host | `localhost` |
42: | Port | `5432` |
43: | Database | `bchat` |
44: | User | `bchat` |
45: | Password | `bchat` |
46: | Full URL | `postgresql://bchat:bchat@localhost:5432/bchat` |

49: 
50: ## Step 1: Validate Migrations Locally
51: 
52: ```bash
53: # Start local Postgres container
54: task -t Taskfile_pg.yml postgres:start
55: 
56: # Validate LATEST.sql + all migrations
57: task -t Taskfile_pg.yml validate:migrations
58: ```
59: 
60: All 4 steps must pass before deploying. See [`docs_testing_pg.md`](docs_testing_pg.md) for details.
61: 
62: ---
63: 
64: ## Step 2: Create Neon Database
65: 
66: 1. Go to https://console.neon.tech
67: 2. Create a new project (region: closest to your Fly.io region)
68: 3. Copy the connection string — it looks like:
69:    ```
70:    postgresql://user:password@ep-xxx.us-east-2.aws.neon.tech/neondb?sslmode=require&channel_binding=require
71:    ```
72: 4. **Keep `sslmode=require`** — Neon requires it
73: 
74: ---
75: 
76: ## Step 3: Set Fly Secrets
77: 
78: **Recommended:** Use the automated script to set all secrets in one session:
79: 
80: ```bash
81: ./scripts/fly-pg-secrets.sh
82: ```
83: 
84: This will prompt for your Neon connection string, OpenRouter API key, and create Tigrisdata S3 storage automatically.
85: 
86: **Manual alternative** — set secrets individually:
87: 
88: ```bash
89: # Database connection string (Neon)
90: fly -a bchat-pg secrets set DATABASE_URL="postgresql://user:password@ep-xxx.us-east-2.aws.neon.tech/neondb?sslmode=require&channel_binding=require"
91: 
92: # LLM API key
93: fly -a bchat-pg secrets set OPENROUTER_API_KEY="sk-or-v1-xxx"
94: 
95: # Encryption key for tenant API keys (auto-generated)
96: fly -a bchat-pg secrets set ENCRYPTION_MASTER_KEY="$(uuidgen)"
97: 
98: # LanceDB S3 storage (Tigrisdata)
99: fly -a bchat-pg secrets set LANCEDB_S3_BUCKET="your-bucket"
100: ```
101: 
102: **Note:** `DATABASE_URL` is read via `os.Getenv()` in `internal/profile/profile.go`, not via viper. It works as a Fly secret without any additional config.
103:

107:

109: fly -a bchat-pg deploy -c fly_pg.toml
110: ```
111: 
112: This builds the Docker image (`Dockerfile.pg.fly`) and deploys to Fly.io.

127: ```

131: ## Configuration Reference
132: 
133: ### fly_pg.toml vs fly.toml
134: 
135: | Setting | `fly.toml` (SQLite) | `fly_pg.toml` (Neon) |
136: |---------|---------------------|----------------------|
137: | App name | `bchat0534` | `bchat-pg` |
138: | `[[mounts]]` | Required (`memos_data`) | **None** — Neon replaces volume |
139: | `MEMOS_DRIVER` | Not set (defaults to sqlite) | `'postgres'` in `[env]` |
140: | `DATABASE_URL` | Not set | Set via `fly secrets set` |
141: | Dockerfile | `Dockerfile.s3.fly` | `Dockerfile.pg.fly` |
142: 
143: ### Env Var Flow (Production)
144: 
145: ```
146: fly secrets set DATABASE_URL="postgresql://..."
147:     ↓
148: Docker container starts, entrypoint.sh runs
149:     ↓
150: bin/memos/main.go → viper reads MEMOS_DRIVER=postgres from env
151:     ↓
152: profile.Validate(): p.DSN == "" → p.DSN = os.Getenv("DATABASE_URL")
153:     ↓
154: store/db/db.go: switch "postgres" → postgres.NewDB(profile)
155:     ↓
156: store/db/postgres/postgres.go: sql.Open("pgx", profile.DSN)
157:     ↓
158: pgx/v5 handles sslmode=require natively for Neon
159: ```
160: 
161: ---
162: 
163: ## S3 Configuration Reference
164: 
165: `Dockerfile.pg.fly` bakes in S3 env vars for Tigrisdata. Only the bucket name needs to be set as a Fly secret.
166: 
167: | Variable | Value | Source |
168: |----------|-------|--------|
169: | `LANCEDB_STORAGE_PROVIDER` | `s3` | `fly_pg.toml` `[env]` |
170: | `LANCEDB_S3_ENDPOINT` | `t3.storage.dev` | Baked into Dockerfile |
171: | `LANCEDB_S3_REGION` | `auto` | Baked into Dockerfile |
172: | `LANCEDB_S3_FORCE_PATH_STYLE` | `false` | Baked into Dockerfile |
173: | `LANCEDB_S3_BUCKET` | Your bucket name | Fly secret |
174: | `AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID` | Tigrisdata credential | Fly secret (auto by `fly storage create`) |
175: | `AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY` | Tigrisdata credential | Fly secret (auto by `fly storage create`) |
176: 
177: ### Create S3 Storage
178: 
179: ```bash
180: # Create Tigrisdata bucket (auto-generates AWS credentials)
181: fly storage create --app bchat-pg
182: 
183: # Set bucket name as secret
184: fly -a bchat-pg secrets set LANCEDB_S3_BUCKET="your-bucket-name"
185: ```
186: 
187: ### Local LanceDB Fallback
188: 
189: If `LANCEDB_S3_BUCKET` is not set or S3 is unreachable, LanceDB falls back to local storage at `/var/opt/memos` (created by `Dockerfile.pg.fly`).
190: 
191: ---
192: 
193: ## Quick Reference
194: 
195: | Action | Command |
196: |--------|---------|
197: | Set all secrets (recommended) | `./scripts/fly-pg-secrets.sh` |
198: | Validate migrations | `task -t Taskfile_pg.yml validate:migrations` |
199: | Start local Postgres | `task -t Taskfile_pg.yml postgres:start` |
200: | Stop local Postgres | `task -t Taskfile_pg.yml postgres:stop` |
201: | Deploy | `fly -a bchat-pg deploy -c fly_pg.toml` |
202: | Check logs | `fly -a bchat-pg logs` |
203: | Set secrets (manual) | `fly -a bchat-pg secrets set KEY=VALUE` |
204: 
205: ---
206: 
207: ## Troubleshooting
208: 
209: ### "unknown db driver"
210: `MEMOS_DRIVER` env var not set. Ensure `fly_pg.toml` has `MEMOS_DRIVER = 'postgres'` in `[env]`.
211: 
212: ### "postgres driver requires DSN or DATABASE_URL"
213: `DATABASE_URL` not set as Fly secret. Run `fly -a bchat-pg secrets set DATABASE_URL="..."`.
214: 
215: ### "failed to ping database"
216: - Check Neon is not paused (free tier autosuspends after ~5 min)
217: - Verify `sslmode=require` in connection string
218: - Check network connectivity
219: 
220: ### Neon cold start delay
221: Free tier databases pause after ~5 min inactivity. First connection takes 2-5s. The 60s ping timeout handles this.
222: 
223: ### LanceDB S3 upload fails
224: Check that `LANCEDB_S3_BUCKET`, `AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID`, and `AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY` are set as Fly secrets. Verify with `fly secrets list --app bchat-pg`.
225: 
226: ### S3 bucket not found
227: Run `fly storage list --app bchat-pg` to see available buckets. If none exist, create one: `fly storage create --app bchat-pg`.
228: 
229: ---
230:

232: *Updated: Added S3 configuration reference and automated secrets script*

(End of file - total 232 lines)
</content>

4: # Build stage

<content>
1: # Testing & Deployment Guide: SQLite vs Postgres
2: 
3: **Date:** 2026-07-08
4: **Status:** Plan
5: 
6: ---
7: 
8: ## Overview
9: 
10: This document clarifies the full lifecycle — build, test, run locally, deploy — for both SQLite and Postgres (Neon) backends. The key insight: **the binary is identical**. The database driver is selected at runtime, not compile time.
11: 
12: | Aspect | SQLite | Postgres |
13: |--------|--------|----------|
14: | Taskfile | `Taskfile.yml` | `Taskfile_pg.yml` |
15: | Build command | `task build` / `task build:rag` | Same (identical binary) |
16: | Run command | `task run` | `task -t Taskfile_pg.yml run` |
17: | Driver selection | Default (`--driver sqlite`) | `MEMOS_DRIVER=postgres` env var |
18: | Migration validation | `task validate:migrations` | `task -t Taskfile_pg.yml validate:migrations` |
19: | Local DB | File: `build/data/memos_dev.db` | Remote Neon or local Docker container |
20: | Deploy config | `fly.toml` + `Dockerfile.s3.fly` | `fly_pg.toml` + `Dockerfile.pg.fly` |
21: | Fly.io volume | Required (`memos_data`) | Not needed (Neon replaces it) |
22: 
23: ---
24: 
25: ## Phase 1: Setup (One-Time)
26: 
27: | Step | SQLite | Postgres |
28: |------|--------|----------|
29: | Install deps | `task setup` | Same |
30: | LanceDB libs | `task setup:lancedb` | Same |
31: | Env file | `cp .env.example .env` + fill `OPENROUTER_API_KEY` | Same, plus add `MEMOS_DRIVER=postgres` and `DATABASE_URL` |
32: | Local Postgres | N/A | `task -t Taskfile_pg.yml postgres:start` |
33: 
34: ---
35: 
36: ## Phase 2: Build
37: 
38: **The build is identical for both databases.** All three drivers (sqlite, postgres, mysql) are compiled into every binary. The `rag` build tag only gates LanceDB vector DB files, not database drivers.
39: 
40: | Command | What it builds | Use for |
41: |---------|---------------|---------|
42: | `task build` | Frontend + Go backend (no RAG) | Quick SQLite testing |
43: | `task build:rag` | Frontend + Go backend with LanceDB | RAG features |
44: | `task build:rag:all` | Frontend + backend + widget + LanceDB | Full build |
45: | `task build:frontend` | React frontend only | Frontend-only iteration |
46: | `task build:backend` | Go binary only (depends on `validate:migrations`) | Backend-only iteration |
47: 
48: **Build dependency chain:** `build:backend` → `validate:migrations` → runs `validate-migrations.sh` (SQLite) or `validate-pg-migrations.sh` (Postgres, if using `Taskfile_pg.yml`).
49: 
50: **Note:** `Taskfile_pg.yml` inherits all build tasks from `Taskfile.yml` via `includes` with `flatten: true`. Only run and validation tasks are overridden.
51: 
52: ---
53: 
54: ## Phase 3: Test
55: 
56: There is **no `task test` command**. Tests are run via raw `go test` or `task validate:schema`.
57: 
58: ### Schema Validation
59: 
60: | Command | Database | What it checks |
61: |---------|----------|---------------|
62: | `task validate:schema` | SQLite | Runs 4 specific tests: `TestSchemaValidation`, `TestAgentSourceFile`, `TestAgentTenantScript`, `TestMigrationHistoryVersion` |
63: | `task validate:migrations` | SQLite | Validates LATEST.sql matches migration files |
64: | `task -t Taskfile_pg.yml validate:migrations` | Postgres | Validates LATEST.sql + all migrations apply cleanly against running Postgres |
65: 
66: ### Store Tests
67: 
68: | Command | Database | Notes |
69: |---------|----------|-------|
70: | `go test -v ./store/test/...` | SQLite (default) | Uses temp DB file, auto-migrates |
71: | `DRIVER=postgres DSN="postgresql://bchat:bchat@localhost:5432/bchat" go test -v ./store/test/...` | Postgres | Requires running Postgres |
72: | `DRIVER=mysql DSN="root@/memos_test" go test -v ./store/test/...` | MySQL | Requires running MySQL |
73: 
74: **Test gating:** Some tests skip based on `DRIVER` env var:
75: - `schema_validation_test.go` — skips unless `DRIVER=""` or `"sqlite"`
76: - `agent_lead_postgres_test.go` — skips unless `DRIVER=postgres`
77: - `bridge_postgres_cascade_test.go` — skips unless `DRIVER=postgres`
78: 
79: ### Agent/Server Tests
80: 
81: | Command | Build tag | Notes |
82: |---------|-----------|-------|
83: | `go test -v ./server/router/api/v1/agent/...` | None | Runs all agent tests (no LanceDB) |
84: | `go test -tags rag -v ./server/router/api/v1/agent/...` | `rag` | Includes LanceDB tests |
85: | `go test -tags "rag integration" -v ./server/router/api/v1/agent/...` | `rag + integration` | Full integration (needs native lib + `LD_LIBRARY_PATH`) |
86: 
87: ### Migration Validation Scripts
88: 
89: | Script | Database | Requires | What it checks |
90: |--------|----------|----------|---------------|
91: | `scripts/validate-migrations.sh` | SQLite | `sqlite3` CLI | LATEST.sql table count matches |
92: | `scripts/validate-db-migrations.sh` | SQLite | `sqlite3` CLI | Numbering, schema, sequencing (used by `fly:db-check`) |
93: | `scripts/validate-pg-migrations.sh` | Postgres | Running Postgres + `psql` | LATEST.sql vs migration schema equivalence |
94: 
95: ---
96: 
97: ## Phase 4: Run Locally
98: 
99: ### SQLite (Taskfile.yml)
100: 
101: | Command | RAG | Embeddings | Storage |
102: |---------|-----|------------|---------|
103: | `task run` | No | N/A | File: `build/data/memos_dev.db` |
104: | `task run:rag` | Yes | `openai/text-embedding-3-small` | Local LanceDB |
105: | `task run:testrag` | Yes | `qwen/qwen3-embedding-8b` | Local LanceDB, force reindex |
106: | `task run:rag:l12` | Yes | `all-MiniLM-L12-v2` (local) | Local LanceDB |
107: | `task run:rag:s3` | Yes | `openai/text-embedding-3-small` | S3/Tigris |
108: 
109: All SQLite run commands pass `--data {{.ROOT_DIR}}/build/data` for the DB file location.
110: 
111: ### Postgres (Taskfile_pg.yml)
112: 
113: | Command | RAG | Embeddings | Storage |
114: |---------|-----|------------|---------|
115: | `task -t Taskfile_pg.yml run` | No | N/A | Neon (via `DATABASE_URL`) |
116: | `task -t Taskfile_pg.yml run:rag` | Yes | `openai/text-embedding-3-small` | Neon + Local LanceDB |
117: | `task -t Taskfile_pg.yml run:testrag` | Yes | `qwen/qwen3-embedding-8b` | Neon + Local LanceDB, force reindex |
118: | `task -t Taskfile_pg.yml run:rag:l12` | Yes | `all-MiniLM-L12-v2` (local) | Neon + Local LanceDB |
119: 
120: All Postgres run commands prepend `MEMOS_DRIVER=postgres` and omit `--data` (Postgres uses `DATABASE_URL`, not a file).
121: 
122: ### Key Differences
123: 
124: | Aspect | SQLite | Postgres |
125: |--------|--------|----------|
126: | `--data` flag | Passed (file path) | Omitted |
127: | `MEMOS_DRIVER` | Not set (defaults to `sqlite`) | Set to `postgres` |
128: | DB location | `build/data/memos_dev.db` | Remote Neon or local Docker |
129: | Startup time | Instant (file open) | ~1-3s (connection + ping) |
130: | Data persistence | File survives restarts | Neon: persists; Docker: persists via volume |
131: 
132: ### Docker Compose (Postgres only)
133: 
134: | Command | Description |
135: |---------|-------------|
136: | `task -t Taskfile_pg.yml postgres:start` | Start local Postgres 16 container |
137: | `task -t Taskfile_pg.yml postgres:stop` | Stop container (data preserved) |
138: | `task -t Taskfile_pg.yml postgres:status` | Show container status |
139: | `task -t Taskfile_pg.yml postgres:logs` | Stream container logs |
140: | `task -t Taskfile_pg.yml postgres:reset` | Destroy and recreate database |
141: 
142: Local Postgres credentials: `postgresql://bchat:bchat@localhost:5432/bchat`
143: 
144: ---
145: 
146: ## Phase 5: Deploy to Fly.io
147: 
148: ### SQLite Deployment
149: 
150: ```bash
151: # Pre-deployment checks
152: task fly:pre-deploy          # Runs fly:check + fly:db-check
153: 
154: # Set secrets
155: fly secrets set OPENROUTER_API_KEY=sk-or-v1-xxx
156: fly secrets set ENCRYPTION_MASTER_KEY=$(uuidgen)
157: 
158: # Create volume (first time only)
159: fly volumes create memos_data --size 1 --region ord
160: 
161: # Deploy
162: fly deploy
163: ```
164: 
165: Config: `fly.toml` + `Dockerfile.s3.fly`
166: 
167: ### Postgres Deployment
168: 
169: ```bash
170: # Pre-deployment checks
171: task -t Taskfile_pg.yml fly:db-check    # Validates Postgres migrations
172: task fly:check                           # Validates env chain
173: 
174: # Set secrets (different app name)
175: fly -a appname secrets set DATABASE_URL="postgresql://..."
176: fly -a appname secrets set OPENROUTER_API_KEY=sk-or-v1-xxx
177: fly -a appname secrets set LANCEDB_S3_BUCKET="your-bucket"
178: # fly -a appname secrets set ENCRYPTION_MASTER_KEY=$(uuidgen)  # optional
179: 
180: # Deploy (no volume needed)
181: fly -a appname deploy -c fly_pg.toml
182: ```
183: 
184: Config: `fly_pg.toml` + `Dockerfile.pg.fly`
185: 
186: ### Deployment Comparison
187: 
188: | Aspect | SQLite | Postgres |
189: |--------|--------|----------|
190: | Config file | `fly.toml` | `fly_pg.toml` |
191: | Dockerfile | `Dockerfile.s3.fly` | `Dockerfile.pg.fly` |
192: | Volume | Required (`memos_data`) | Not needed |
193: | `DATABASE_URL` | Not set | Set via `fly secrets set` |
194: | `MEMOS_DRIVER` | Not set (defaults to sqlite) | In `fly_pg.toml` `[env]` |
195: | App name | `appname` | `appname` (separate app) |
196: | Pre-deploy check | `task fly:pre-deploy` | `task -t Taskfile_pg.yml fly:db-check` |
197: 
198: ### fly.toml Variants (Stale)
199: 
200: The following files are **stale/unused** and should not be used for new deployments:
201: 
202: | File | Status | Notes |
203: |------|--------|-------|
204: | `fly.s3.toml` | Stale | Same app as `fly.toml`, different embedding model |
205: | `fly.local.toml` | Stale | Uses local LanceDB storage |
206: | `fly_prod.toml` | Stale | Uses deepinfra embeddings, different LLM |
207: | `fly copy.toml` | Stale | Backup of older local config |
208: 
209: Only `fly.toml` (SQLite) and `fly_pg.toml` (Postgres) are active.
210: 
211: ---
212: 
213: ## Quick Reference: SQLite vs Postgres Commands
214: 
215: | Action | SQLite | Postgres |
216: |--------|--------|----------|
217: | Build | `task build:rag` | `task build:rag` (same) |
218: | Validate migrations | `task validate:migrations` | `task -t Taskfile_pg.yml validate:migrations` |
219: | Run dev server | `task run` | `task -t Taskfile_pg.yml run` |
220: | Run with RAG | `task run:rag` | `task -t Taskfile_pg.yml run:rag` |
221: | Start local DB | N/A (file-based) | `task -t Taskfile_pg.yml postgres:start` |
222: | Run store tests | `go test -v ./store/test/...` | `DRIVER=postgres DSN="..." go test -v ./store/test/...` |
223: | Validate env chain | `task fly:check` | `task fly:check` (same) |
224: | Pre-deploy check | `task fly:pre-deploy` | `task -t Taskfile_pg.yml fly:db-check` |
225: | Deploy | `fly deploy` | `fly -a appname deploy -c fly_pg.toml` |
226: 
227: ---

191: func (r *agentServiceForRotation) ReEncryptOnStartup(ctx context.Context) error {
192: 	p := &profile.Profile{EncryptionMasterKey: r.primaryKey}
193: 	svc := agent.NewService(r.store, p)
194: 	succeeded, failed, reErr := svc.ReEncryptOnStartup(ctx)
195: 	if reErr != nil {
196: 		slog.Error("key rotation aborted", "error", reErr)
197: 		return fmt.Errorf("key rotation aborted: %w", reErr)
198: 	}
199: 	if failed > 0 {
200: 		slog.Error("key rotation completed with failures", "succeeded", succeeded, "failed", failed)
201: 		return fmt.Errorf("key rotation partially failed: %d of %d secrets not re-encrypted", failed, succeeded+failed)
202: 	}
203: 	slog.Info("Key rotation complete", "re_encrypted", succeeded)
204: 	return nil
205: }

317: // getOrCreateEncryptionKey reads or generates a UUID-based encryption key.
318: // The key file is single-instance per data dir. We must NEVER fall back to a
319: // locally generated key when the file already exists but is empty/short (e.g.
320: // a crash between O_EXCL create and write) or when another instance won the
321: // O_EXCL race — doing so produces divergent master keys and silent, permanent
322: // loss of all previously encrypted tenant secrets (M7 / H2).
323: func getOrCreateEncryptionKey(dataDir string) string {
324: 	keyFile := filepath.Join(dataDir, ".encryption_key")
325: 	if data, err := os.ReadFile(keyFile); err == nil {
326: 		key := strings.TrimSpace(string(data))
327: 		if len(key) >= 16 {
328: 			return key
329: 		}
330: 		// Existing file is corrupt/empty (crashed writer) and we own it (we just
331: 		// read it and decided to regenerate). Heal it so we can claim the slot.
332: 		slog.Warn("existing encryption key file is empty or too short; it will be regenerated", "file", keyFile)
333: 		if rmErr := os.Remove(keyFile); rmErr != nil {
334: 			// If we cannot clear the corrupt file we must not proceed to an O_EXCL
335: 			// that will fail and panic anyway — fail loudly here.
336: 			slog.Error("cannot clear corrupt encryption key file; aborting startup", "file", keyFile, "error", rmErr)
337: 			panic(fmt.Sprintf("cannot clear corrupt encryption key file %s: %v", keyFile, rmErr))
338: 		}
339: 	}
340: 
341: 	key := uuid.New().String()
342: 	if err := os.MkdirAll(dataDir, 0700); err != nil {
343: 		slog.Warn("failed to create data directory for encryption key", "error", err)
344: 		return key
345: 	}
346: 
347: 	// Retry once in case another instance holds the slot transiently.
348: 	for attempt := 0; attempt < 2; attempt++ {
349: 		f, err := os.OpenFile(keyFile, os.O_WRONLY|os.O_CREATE|os.O_EXCL, 0600)
350: 		if err != nil {
351: 			// Another instance won the race — adopt its (valid) key.
352: 			if data, readErr := os.ReadFile(keyFile); readErr == nil {
353: 				if k := strings.TrimSpace(string(data)); len(k) >= 16 {
354: 					return k
355: 				}
356: 			}
357: 			// The peer's file is empty/short because it is still crashing. We must
358: 			// NOT remove it — that would unlink a peer's in-flight key and let us
359: 			// create a DIVERGENT key (F1). Just retry; the peer will finish writing
360: 			// and a later ReadFile will adopt its valid key.
361: 			slog.Warn("encryption key file claimed by a peer is unusable; will retry", "error", err)
362: 			continue
363: 		}
364: 		if _, wErr := f.WriteString(key + "\n"); wErr != nil {
365: 			f.Close()
366: 			// Do not leave a partial/empty file behind.
367: 			_ = os.Remove(keyFile)
368: 			slog.Warn("failed to write encryption key file", "error", wErr)
369: 			return key
370: 		}
371: 		if fErr := f.Close(); fErr != nil {
372: 			slog.Warn("failed to close encryption key file", "error", fErr)
373: 		}
374: 		slog.Info("Generated new encryption key", "file", keyFile)
375: 		return key
376: 	}
377: 
378: 	// Last resort: another instance keeps winning with a valid file — adopt it.
379: 	if data, readErr := os.ReadFile(keyFile); readErr == nil {
380: 		if k := strings.TrimSpace(string(data)); len(k) >= 16 {
381: 			return k
382: 		}
383: 	}
384: 	// We could not establish a stable key that matches the on-disk file. Returning
385: 	// a locally generated key here would create divergent master keys across
386: 	// processes and silently, permanently lose tenant secrets. Abort instead.
387: 	slog.Error("unable to establish a stable encryption key file; tenant secret encryption may be inconsistent")
388: 	panic("unable to establish a stable encryption key file; refusing to start with a divergent master key")
389: }

455:## File descriptors limit
457:CockroachDB can use a large number of open file descriptors, often more than is available by default. Therefore, note the following recommendations.
461:* At a **minimum**, the file descriptors limit must be `1956` (1700 per store plus 256 for networking). If the limit is below this threshold, the node will not start.
462:* It is **recommended** to set the file descriptors limit to `unlimited`; otherwise, the recommended limit is at least `15000` (10000 per store plus 5000 for networking). This higher limit ensures performance and accommodates cluster growth.
463:* When the file descriptors limit is not high enough to allocate the recommended amounts, CockroachDB allocates 10000 per store and the rest for networking; if this would result in networking getting less than 256, CockroachDB instead allocates 256 for networking and evenly splits the rest across stores.

## Connect to a CockroachDB Cluster

This page documents the required connection configuration for [fully-supported third-party tools](https://www.cockroachlabs.com/docs/v26.2/third-party-database-tools).

For a list of all supported cluster connection parameters, see the [`cockroach` Connection Parameters](https://www.cockroachlabs.com/docs/v26.2/connection-parameters).

### Step 1. Select your deployment

CockroachDB Basic/Standard
CockroachDB Advanced
CockroachDB self-hosted

To connect to a CockroachDB Cloud cluster, you need a general connection string or connection parameters, which include the username, host, database, and port. To connect to a CockroachDB self-hosted cluster, you need the [general connection string](https://www.cockroachlabs.com/docs/v26.2/connection-parameters#connect-using-a-url) or [connection parameters](https://www.cockroachlabs.com/docs/v26.2/connection-parameters#connect-using-discrete-parameters) for your cluster.

Warning:
PostgreSQL connection URIs do not support special characters. If you have special characters in your password, you will have to [URL encode](https://www.w3schools.com/tags/ref_urlencode.ASP) them (e.g., `password!` should be entered as `password%21`) to connect to your cluster.

Note:
If you forget your SQL user's password, an [Organization Admin](https://www.cockroachlabs.com/docs/cockroachcloud/authorization#organization-admin) or a Cluster Admin on the cluster can change the password on the **SQL Users** page.

1. In the top right corner of the CockroachDB Cloud Console, click **Connect**.

The **Setup** page of the **Connect to cluster** dialog displays.
2\. If you have set up a private connection, select it to connect privately. Otherwise, click **IP Allowlist**.
3\. Select the **SQL User**. If you have only one SQL user, it is automatically selected.

- [Build a Python App with CockroachDB](https://www.cockroachlabs.com/docs/v26.2/build-a-python-app-with-cockroachdb)
- [Build a Go App with CockroachDB](https://www.cockroachlabs.com/docs/v26.2/build-a-go-app-with-cockroachdb)
- [Build a Java App with CockroachDB](https://www.cockroachlabs.com/docs/v26.2/build-a-java-app-with-cockroachdb)
- [Build a Ruby App with CockroachDB](https://www.cockroachlabs.com/docs/v26.2/build-a-ruby-app-with-cockroachdb)
- [Build a Javascript App with CockroachDB](https://www.cockroachlabs.com/docs/v26.2/build-a-nodejs-app-with-cockroachdb)

1. If you need to download the CA certificate, first set **Select option/language** to **General Connection String** and expand the **Download CA Cert** section. In the **Download CA Cert** section of the dialog, select your operating system, and use the command provided to download the CA certificate to the default PostgreSQL certificate directory on your machine.
1. Select the **Parameters only** option of the **Select option/language** dropdown.
1. Use the connection parameters provided in the dialog to connect to your cluster using a [CockroachDB-compatible tool](https://www.cockroachlabs.com/docs/v26.2/third-party-database-tools).
| Parameter | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `{username}` | The [SQL user](https://www.cockroachlabs.com/docs/cockroachcloud/managing-access#create-a-sql-user) connecting to the cluster. |
| `{host}` | The host on which the CockroachDB node is running. |
| `{port}` | The port at which the CockroachDB node is listening. |

# Docs > Cockroachcloud > Connect to a CockroachDB Basic Cluster
## Connect to your cluster

1. Select your cluster to navigate to the cluster [**Overview** page](https://www.cockroachlabs.com/docs/cockroachcloud/overview-page).
1. In the top right corner of the CockroachDB Cloud Console, click the **Connect** button.

The **Connect to cluster** dialog displays.
3\. *(Optional)* If you have multiple SQL users or databases, you can:

\* Select the SQL user you want to connect with from the **SQL user** dropdown.
\* Select the database you want to connect to from the **Database** dropdown.
4\. Select a connection method from the **Select option / Language** dropdown (the instructions below will adjust accordingly):

Command line
General connection string
Connection parameters

1. In the **Download CA Cert** section of the dialog, you can optionally download the CA certificate. The CA certificate is signed by Let's Encrypt, which may already be trusted by your local system. However, some use cases, such as developing with Python, do not use the operating system's local certificate store and require the CA certificate to be available locally. When developing with Javascript or Node, you do not need to download the CA certificate locally. To download the CA certificate, select your operating system, then use the command provided to download the CA certificate to the default PostgreSQL certificate directory on your machine.
1. Copy the connection string provided in the **General connection string** section of the dialog, which will be used to connect your application to your cluster.
1. Add your copied connection string to your application code. For information about connecting to your cluster with a [supported client](https://www.cockroachlabs.com/docs/v26.2/third-party-database-tools), see [Connect to a CockroachDB Cluster](https://www.cockroachlabs.com/docs/v26.2/connect-to-the-database).

Warning:
PostgreSQL connection URIs do not support special characters. If you have special characters in your password, you will have to [URL encode](https://www.w3schools.com/tags/ref_urlencode.ASP) them (e.g., `password!` should be entered as `password%21`) to connect to your cluster.

Note:
If you forget your SQL user's password, an [Organization Admin](https://www.cockroachlabs.com/docs/cockroachcloud/authorization#organization-admin) or a Cluster Admin on the cluster can change the password on the **SQL Users** page.

For connection examples and code snippets in your language, see the following:

- [Build a Python App with CockroachDB](https://www.cockroachlabs.com/docs/v26.2/build-a-python-app-with-cockroachdb)
- [Build a Go App with CockroachDB](https://www.cockroachlabs.com/docs/v26.2/build-a-go-app-with-cockroachdb)
- [Build a Java App with CockroachDB](https://www.cockroachlabs.com/docs/v26.2/build-a-java-app-with-cockroachdb)
- [Build a Ruby App with CockroachDB](https://www.cockroachlabs.com/docs/v26.2/build-a-ruby-app-with-cockroachdb)
- [Build a Javascript App with CockroachDB](https://www.cockroachlabs.com/docs/v26.2/build-a-nodejs-app-with-cockroachdb)

1. If you need to download the CA certificate, first set **Select option/language** to **General Connection String** and expand the **Downloada CA Cert** section. In the **Download CA Cert** section of the dialog, select your operating system, and use the command provided to download the CA certificate to the default PostgreSQL certificate directory on your machine.
1. Select the **Parameters only** option of the **Select option** dropdown.
1. Use the connection parameters provided in the dialog to connect to your cluster using a [CockroachDB-compatible tool](https://www.cockroachlabs.com/docs/v26.2/third-party-database-tools).

# Docs > Cockroachcloud > Connect to a CockroachDB Advanced Cluster
## Connect to your cluster

1. In the top right corner of the CockroachDB Cloud Console, click **Connect**.

The **Setup** page of the **Connect to cluster** dialog displays.
2\. If you set up a private connection, select it to connect privately. Otherwise, click **IP Allowlist**.
3\. Select the **SQL User**. If you have only one SQL user, it is automatically selected.

Note:
If you forget your SQL user's password, an [Organization Admin](https://www.cockroachlabs.com/docs/cockroachcloud/authorization#organization-admin) or a Cluster Admin on the cluster can change the password on the **SQL Users** page.
4\. Select the **Database**. If you have only one database, it is automatically selected.
5\. For a multi-region cluster, select the **Region** to connect to. If you have only one region, it is automatically selected.
6\. Click **Next**.

The **Connect** page of the **Connection info** dialog displays.
7\. In the dialog, select the tab for a connection method, then follow the instructions below for that method.

Command line
Connection string
Connection parameters

You can connect to your cluster with any [supported version](https://www.cockroachlabs.com/docs/releases/release-support-policy#supported-versions) of the full CockroachDB binary or the [built-in SQL client](https://www.cockroachlabs.com/docs/v26.2/cockroach-sql). To download the full binary and connect to a CockroachDB Advanced cluster, follow these steps.

Tip:
To download a supported version of the SQL shell instead of the full binary, visit [Releases](https://cockroachlabs.com/releases).

1. Select the **Command Line** tab.
1. If CockroachDB is not installed locally, copy the command to download and install it. In your terminal, run the command.
1. If the CA certificate for the cluster is not downloaded locally, copy the command to download it. In your terminal, run the command.
1. Copy the [`cockroach sql`](https://www.cockroachlabs.com/docs/v26.2/cockroach-sql) command, which will be used in the next step (and to connect to your cluster in the future). Click **Close**.
1. In your terminal, enter the copied `cockroach sql` command and connection string to start the [built-in SQL client](https://www.cockroachlabs.com/docs/v26.2/cockroach-sql).
1. Enter the SQL user's password and enter.

Warning:
PostgreSQL connection URIs do not support special characters. If you have special characters in your password, you will have to [URL encode](https://www.w3schools.com/tags/ref_urlencode.ASP) them (e.g., `password!` should be entered as `password%21`) to connect to your cluster.

A welcome message displays:

```

 Welcome to the CockroachDB SQL shell.
 All statements must be terminated by a semicolon.
 To exit, type: \q.


```

You are now connected to the built-in SQL client, and can now run [CockroachDB SQL statements](https://www.cockroachlabs.com/docs/v26.2/sql-statements).

To connect to your cluster from your application:

1. Select the **Connection string** tab.
1. If the CA certificate for the cluster is not downloaded locally, copy the command to download it. In your terminal, run the command.
1. Copy the connection string, which begins with `postgresql://`. This will be used to connect your application to CockroachDB Advanced.
1. Add your copied connection string to your application code. For information about connecting to CockroachDB Advanced with a [supported client](https://www.cockroachlabs.com/docs/v26.2/third-party-database-tools), see [Connect to a CockroachDB Cluster](https://www.cockroachlabs.com/docs/v26.2/connect-to-the-database).
1. Click **Close**.

Warning:
PostgreSQL connection URIs do not support special characters. If you have special characters in your password, you will have to [URL encode](https://www.w3schools.com/tags/ref_urlencode.ASP) them (e.g., `password!` should be entered as `password%21`) to connect to your cluster.

# Docs > Cockroachcloud > Network Authorization for CockroachDB Cloud
## IP allowlisting

Authorized network access can be managed from the CockroachDB Cloud console Network Authorization page at:

`https://cockroachlabs.cloud/cluster/{ your cluster UUID}/networking`

Standard and Advanced clusters support different maximum numbers of IP allowlist rules:
| Cluster Type | IP allowlist rule max |
| --- | --- |
| Advanced (AWS) | 20 |
| Advanced (GCP and Azure) | 200 |
| Standard or Basic | 50 |

If you need to add more than the maximum number of allowlist rules, [contact Support](https://support.cockroachlabs.com).

Note:
While developing and testing your application, you may add `0.0.0.0/0` to the allowlist, which allows all networks. However, before moving into production, it is recommenced that you remove the `0.0.0.0/0` network from the allowlist.

If your application servers’ IP addresses are not static, or you want to limit your cluster's exposure to the public network, you can connect to a CockroachDB Advanced cluster privately instead.

Refer to:

- [Connect to a CockroachDB Basic Cluster: Authorize your network](https://www.cockroachlabs.com/docs/cockroachcloud/connect-to-a-basic-cluster#authorize-your-network).
- - [Connect to a CockroachDB Standard Cluster: Authorize your network](https://www.cockroachlabs.com/docs/cockroachcloud/connect-to-your-cluster#authorize-your-network).
- [Connect to a CockroachDB Advanced Cluster: Authorize your network](https://www.cockroachlabs.com/docs/cockroachcloud/connect-to-an-advanced-cluster#authorize-your-network).

# Docs > Cockroachcloud
## CockroachDB Cloud Security Overview

This page summarizes the security features available in CockroachDB Cloud:

- CockroachDB Standard: Deployed in shared (multi-tenant) network and compute infrastructure. Storage scales automatically according to demand, but the cluster's compute requirements are defined explicitly as part of the cluster's configuration.
- CockroachDB Basic: Deployed in shared (multi-tenant) network and compute infrastructure. Storage and compute scale automatically according to demand, and you are charged only for the storage and activity of your cluster.
- CockroachDB Advanced: Deployed in dedicated network and compute infrastructure. This deployment may be distributed over multiple regions for added disaster-resilience. In addition to infrastructure isolation, Advanced clusters can be customized with advanced network, identity-management, and encryption-related security features required for high benchmark security goals such as [PCI DSS compliance](https://www.cockroachlabs.com/docs/cockroachcloud/pci-dss). Refer to [Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard (PCI DSS) Compliance in CockroachDB Advanced](https://www.cockroachlabs.com/docs/cockroachcloud/pci-dss)

| Security Domain | CockroachDB Basic | CockroachDB Standard | CockroachDB Advanced | Feature |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |

# CockroachDB Pricing

The cloud-native, distributed SQL database

![wingbug2023@4x 12](https://images.ctfassets.net/00voh0j35590/4exUIruXHzDqNlWZtBAdd3/07a0059e1e1e27ea81f3523e1b359559/wingbug2023_4x_12.svg)
CockroachDB Cloud[CockroachDB Bring your own cloud](https://www.cockroachlabs.com/product/cloud/bring-your-own-cloud/)CockroachDB Self-HostedCockroachDB CloudCockroachDB Self-Hosted[CockroachDB Bring your own cloud](https://www.cockroachlabs.com/product/cloud/bring-your-own-cloud/)Compare CockroachDB pricing plansBasic

Starts at $0 / monthFor smaller, bursty workloads up to 30K RU/sec (~60 vCPUs).

- 50 million RUs and 10 GiB storage free per month
- On-demand compute and storage that scales to zero
- AWS and GCP multi-region support for select regions
- IP allowlist access control
- 99.99% availability
- Integration of vector data with transactional data
- Includes MCP, CLI and Agent Skills
  View pricingStandard

Preview2 vCPUs start at $0.18 / hrFor steady workloads at scale, up to 200 vCPUs.

- Provisioned compute with instant scaling up to 200 vCPUs, and on-demand storage
- AWS and GCP multi-region support for select regions
- Private connectivity
- Metrics and log export to DataDog
- 99.99% availability
- Integration of vector data with transactional data
- Includes MCP, CLI and Agent Skills
  View pricingAdvanced

4 vCPUs start at $0.60 / hrFor high-scale applications with advanced security and compliance requirements.

- Provisioned compute and storage with unlimited scaling
- AWS, GCP and Azure multi-region support for all regions
- Private connectivity
- Metrics and log export to Datadog
- Up to 99.999% availability
- CMEK and other controls for your PCI / HIPAA needs
- Integration of vector data with transactional data
- Includes MCP, CLI and Agent Skills
  View pricingTry free with $400 in credits. No credit card required for Basic and Standard plans.

CockroachDB Cloud customers with annual or multi-year contracts entered into prior to December 1, 2024 can view legacy pricing [here](https://www.cockroachlabs.com/pricing/legacy/) (effective until their renewal).

# Docs > V23.1 > Security-reference > CockroachDB Security Overview
## Comparison of security features

| Security Domain | Basic | Standard | Advanced | self-hosted Enterprise | Feature |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [Authentication](https://www.cockroachlabs.com/docs/v23.1/security-reference/authentication) | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | Inter-node and node identity authentication using TLS 1.3 |
| ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | Client identity authentication using username/password |
| ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | [SASL/SCRAM-SHA-256 secure password-based authentication](https://www.cockroachlabs.com/docs/v23.1/security-reference/scram-authentication) |
|  |  |  | ✓ | SQL client identity authentication using TLS 1.2/1.3 |
| ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | Web console authentication with third-party [Single Sign-on (SSO)](https://www.cockroachlabs.com/docs/v23.1/sso-db-console) using [OpenID Connect OIDC](https://openid.net/connect/) |
|  |  |  | ✓ | Client identity authentication with [GSSAPI and Kerberos](https://www.cockroachlabs.com/docs/v23.1/gssapi_authentication) |
|  |  |  | ✓ | HTTP API access using login tokens |
|  |  |  | ✓ | [OCSP](https://wikipedia.org/wiki/Online_Certificate_Status_Protocol) certificate revocation protocol |
| [Encryption](https://www.cockroachlabs.com/docs/v23.1/security-reference/encryption) | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | Encryption in transit using TLS 1.3 |
| ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | Backups for AWS clusters are encrypted at rest using [AWS S3’s server-side encryption](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/dev/UsingServerSideEncryption.html) |
| ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | Backups for GCP clusters are encrypted at rest using [Google-managed server-side encryption keys](https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs/encryption/default-keys) |
| ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | Industry-standard encryption at rest is provided at the infrastructure level by your chosen deployment environment, such as Google Cloud Platform (GCP), Amazon Web Services (AWS), or Microsoft Azure. You can learn more about [GCP persistent disk encryption](https://cloud.google.com/compute/docs/disks#pd_encryption), [AWS Elastic Block Storage](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/EBSEncryption.html), or [Azure managed disk encryption](https://docs.microsoft.com/azure/virtual-machines/disk-encryption-overview). |
|  |  |  | ✓ | Cockroach Labs's proprietary storage-level [Enterprise Encryption At Rest service](https://www.cockroachlabs.com/docs/v23.1/security-reference/encryption#encryption-at-rest-enterprise) implementing the [Advanced Encryption Standard (AES)](https://wikipedia.org/wiki/Advanced_Encryption_Standard) |
| [Authorization](https://www.cockroachlabs.com/docs/v23.1/security-reference/authorization) | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | Users and privileges |
| ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | Role-based access control (RBAC) |
| Network Security | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | SQL-level configuration allowed authentication attempts by IP address |
| ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | Network-level Configuration of allowed IP addresses |
|  | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | [GCP Private Service Connect (PSC)](https://www.cockroachlabs.com/docs/cockroachcloud/connect-to-your-cluster#gcp-private-service-connect) or [VPC Peering](https://www.cockroachlabs.com/docs/cockroachcloud/connect-to-your-cluster#vpc-peering) for GCP clusters and [AWS PrivateLink](https://www.cockroachlabs.com/docs/cockroachcloud/aws-privatelink) for AWS clusters |
| [Non-Repudiation](https://wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-repudiation) | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | [SQL Audit Logging](https://www.cockroachlabs.com/docs/v23.1/sql-audit-logging) |
| [Availability/Resilience](https://www.cockroachlabs.com/docs/v23.1/demo-fault-tolerance-and-recovery) | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | CockroachDB, as a distributed SQL database, is uniquely resilient by nature. A cluster can tolerate node failures as long as the majority of nodes remain functional. See [Disaster Recovery.](https://www.cockroachlabs.com/docs/v23.1/demo-fault-tolerance-and-recovery) |

# Docs > Cockroachcloud > Network Authorization for CockroachDB Cloud
## IP allowlisting

Authorized network access can be managed from the CockroachDB Cloud console Network Authorization page at:

`https://cockroachlabs.cloud/cluster/{ your cluster UUID}/networking`

Standard and Advanced clusters support different maximum numbers of IP allowlist rules:
| Cluster Type | IP allowlist rule max |
| --- | --- |
| Advanced (AWS) | 20 |
| Advanced (GCP and Azure) | 200 |
| Standard or Basic | 50 |

If you need to add more than the maximum number of allowlist rules, [contact Support](https://support.cockroachlabs.com).

Note:
While developing and testing your application, you may add `0.0.0.0/0` to the allowlist, which allows all networks. However, before moving into production, it is recommenced that you remove the `0.0.0.0/0` network from the allowlist.

If your application servers’ IP addresses are not static, or you want to limit your cluster's exposure to the public network, you can connect to a CockroachDB Advanced cluster privately instead.

Refer to:

- [Connect to a CockroachDB Basic Cluster: Authorize your network](https://www.cockroachlabs.com/docs/cockroachcloud/connect-to-a-basic-cluster#authorize-your-network).
- - [Connect to a CockroachDB Standard Cluster: Authorize your network](https://www.cockroachlabs.com/docs/cockroachcloud/connect-to-your-cluster#authorize-your-network).
- [Connect to a CockroachDB Advanced Cluster: Authorize your network](https://www.cockroachlabs.com/docs/cockroachcloud/connect-to-an-advanced-cluster#authorize-your-network).

# Docs > Cockroachcloud
## Network Authorization for CockroachDB Cloud

To prevent denial-of-service attacks, brute force password attacks, and other forms of malicious activity, Cockroach Labs recommends restricting your network to allow access only from specific IP address ranges controlled by your organization. These might include specific networks for your application deployments, hardened administrator access points, or disaster recovery pipelines.

This page describes these options and how they help to protect clusters in CockroachDB Cloud.

### Options for controlling network access

You can authorize network access to your cluster by:

- [Adding an authorized range of public IP addresses](https://www.cockroachlabs.com/docs/cockroachcloud/network-authorization#ip-allowlisting).

- Setting up private connectivity so that inbound connections to your cluster from your cloud tenant are made over the cloud provider's private network rather than over the public internet, for enhanced network security and reduced network latency. Available for CockroachDB Advanced and CockroachDB Standard. If you use IP allowlisting rules together with private connectivity, private networks do not need to be added to that allowlist.

  - CockroachDB Advanced or Standard clusters deployed on GCP can connect privately using GCP Private Service Connect (PSC) or GCP VPC peering. PSC allows you to connect your cluster directly to a VPC within your Google Cloud project, while VPC Peering allows you to peer your cluster's VPC in CockroachDB Cloud to a VPC within your Google Cloud project.
  - CockroachDB Advanced or Standard clusters deployed on AWS can connect privately using AWS PrivateLink, which allows you to connect your cluster to a VPC within your AWS account.
  - CockroachDB Advanced clusters deployed on Azure can connect privately using Azure Private Link, which allows you to connect your cluster to a virtual network within your Azure tenant.For detailed instructions, refer to [Establish private connectivity](https://www.cockroachlabs.com/docs/cockroachcloud/connect-to-your-cluster#establish-private-connectivity).

Note:
[VPC Peering](https://www.cockroachlabs.com/docs/cockroachcloud/network-authorization#vpc-peering) and [AWS PrivateLink](https://www.cockroachlabs.com/docs/cockroachcloud/network-authorization#aws-privatelink) in CockroachDB Advanced clusters do **not** support connecting to a [Kafka](https://www.cockroachlabs.com/docs/v26.2/changefeed-sinks#kafka) sink's internal IP addresses for [changefeeds](https://www.cockroachlabs.com/docs/v26.2/change-data-capture-overview). To connect to a Kafka sink from CockroachDB Advanced, it is necessary to expose the Kafka cluster's external IP address and open ports with firewall rules to allow access from the cluster.

**Prerequisite**: Either the [Cluster Operator](https://www.cockroachlabs.com/docs/cockroachcloud/authorization#cluster-operator) or [Cluster Admin](https://www.cockroachlabs.com/docs/cockroachcloud/authorization#cluster-admin) role on an existing cluster, or the [Cluster Creator](https://www.cockroachlabs.com/docs/cockroachcloud/authorization#cluster-creator) role in order to create a new cluster.

Use private connectivity if:

- You need to allowlist more defined IP address ranges than the [default maximum](https://www.cockroachlabs.com/docs/cockroachcloud/network-authorization#ip-allowlisting).
- Your servers’ IP addresses are not static.
- You have a requirement to avoid exposing your cluster to the public internet.

Learn more about [Private Clusters (Preview)](https://www.cockroachlabs.com/docs/cockroachcloud/private-clusters), which offer enhanced cluster security. A private cluster's nodes have no public IP addresses.

Note:
Neither Azure Private Link nor private clusters are available for [CockroachDB Advanced on Azure](https://www.cockroachlabs.com/docs/cockroachcloud/cockroachdb-advanced-on-azure).

# Docs > Cockroachcloud
## Connect to a CockroachDB Advanced Cluster

[CockroachDB Basic](https://www.cockroachlabs.com/docs/cockroachcloud/connect-to-a-basic-cluster)
[CockroachDB Standard](https://www.cockroachlabs.com/docs/cockroachcloud/connect-to-your-cluster)
[CockroachDB Advanced](https://www.cockroachlabs.com/docs/cockroachcloud/connect-to-an-advanced-cluster)

This page shows you how to connect to your CockroachDB Advanced cluster. This includes the administrative task of configuring allowed networks to support SQL client connections, as well as the steps for connecting to the cluster with CockroachDB's [built-in SQL client](https://www.cockroachlabs.com/docs/v26.2/cockroach-sql).

### Before you start

- [Create a cluster](https://www.cockroachlabs.com/docs/cockroachcloud/create-your-cluster).
- [Create a SQL user](https://www.cockroachlabs.com/docs/cockroachcloud/managing-access#create-a-sql-user).
- Understand [Network Authorization for CockroachDB Cloud Clusters](https://www.cockroachlabs.com/docs/cockroachcloud/network-authorization)

### Authorize your network

By default, CockroachDB Advanced clusters are locked down to all network access. You must authorized certain network connections in order to allow SQL clients to connect to your clusters. Advanced clusters can accept connections via two types of authorized network:

- IP allowlisting: Selectively IP address ranges to connect to the cluster.
- Private connectivity: Cloud-provider-specific private networking options, including GCP Private Service Connect, GCP VPC Peering, AWS Privatelink, or Azure Private Link.

Note:
Removing or adding an authorized network on your CockroachDB Advanced cluster may take a few seconds to take effect.

Note:
IPv6 addresses are currently not supported.

To prevent denial-of-service attacks, brute force password attacks, and other forms of malicious activity, it is recommended to restrict your cluster network to allow access only from specific IP address ranges controlled by your organization, corresponding to, for example, your application deployments, hardened administrator access points, or disaster recovery pipelines.

#### Add IP addresses to the allowlist

1. Navigate to your cluster's **Networking > IP Allowlist** tab.

The **IP Allowlist** tab displays a list of authorized networks (i.e., an IP network allowlist) that can access the cluster.
2\. If the network is not listed, authorize it:

1\. Click the **Add Network** button. The **Add Network** dialog displays.
2\. *(Optional)* Enter a **Network name**.
3\. From the **Network** dropdown, select:
\* **New Network** to authorize the network of your local machine or application deployment or another valid source. Enter the public IPv4 address of the source machine in the **Network** field. To add a range of source IP addresses, use the CIDR (Classless Inter-Domain Routing) notation. For a general introduction to IP routing, refer to [Digital Ocean—Understanding IP Addresses, Subnets, and CIDR Notation for Networking](https://www.digitalocean.com/community/tutorials/understanding-ip-addresses-subnets-and-cidr-notation-for-networking#cidr-notation).
\* **Current Network** to auto-populate your local machine's IP address.
\* **Public (Insecure)** to allow all networks, use `0.0.0.0/0`. Use this with caution as your cluster will be vulnerable to denial-of-service and brute force password attacks.
3\. Select whether the network can connect to the cluster's **DB Console to monitor the cluster**, **CockroachDB Client to access databases**, or both.

The DB Console is where you can observe your cluster's health and performance. For more information, see [DB Console Overview](https://www.cockroachlabs.com/docs/v26.2/ui-overview).
4\. Click **Apply**.
